article.overview: A neutral mass spectrometer identifies the chemical species present in a thin gas by first ionising its electrically neutral particles and then sorting the resulting ions by mass-to-charge ratio. On the Moon it is used to measure the composition and variability of the lunar exosphere, the extremely tenuous atmosphere that surrounds the Moon. This article covers three flown examples: the Apollo 17 Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment (LACE), the LADEE Neutral Mass Spectrometer (NMS) and the CHACE-2 instrument on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter. The payload name describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design, so the specifications of each example must be read separately.
article.description: A neutral mass spectrometer has three main functional stages. An inlet admits gas from the surrounding environment, an ionisation source converts neutral molecules and atoms into ions, usually by electron impact, and a mass analyser separates those ions according to their mass-to-charge ratio. A detector then counts the ions at each mass, and electronics convert the counts into a spectrum that scientists can interpret. The inlet and ionisation source determine which gases can be sampled efficiently, while the analyser sets the mass range and resolution. Three different analyser designs are represented in this article. The Apollo 17 LACE used a miniature magnetic-deflection analyser. The LADEE NMS and the CHACE-2 instrument are both described as quadrupole mass spectrometers. Each design has different strengths in mass range, resolution, sensitivity and size, so the instruments are not directly interchangeable.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar neutral mass spectrometer is to determine which gas species are present in the exosphere, in what abundance, and how those abundances change in space and time. The Moon's exosphere is far thinner than Earth's atmosphere, so direct sampling by an instrument on or near the surface, or in lunar orbit, is one of the few ways to measure it. The LADEE NMS was planned to determine the abundance of several exospheric species, to lower the existing upper limits for many others, and to reveal spatial and temporal patterns. Its planned targets included species that condense at night and peak near the dawn terminator, possible episodic release from the lunar interior, and the effects of sputtering and desorption from the regolith. The CHACE-2 instrument was designed to map the global distribution of argon-40 in the exosphere, to study the dynamics of exospheric species, and to gain insight into radiogenic activity in the first few tens of metres below the surface. Argon-40 is a radiogenic gas, produced by the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in the Moon's crust, so its distribution can carry information about the subsurface. The Apollo 17 LACE was designed to study the composition of the lunar atmosphere and its variations, and it was a follow-on to earlier cold-cathode gauge measurements on Apollo 14 and 15.
article.operating_principle: In a quadrupole mass spectrometer, neutral gas molecules enter an ionisation chamber where electrons bombard them and produce positive ions. The ions are then accelerated into a quadrupole field made of four parallel rods with combined direct-current and radio-frequency voltages. For a given set of voltages, only ions of one mass-to-charge ratio follow a stable path through the rods and reach the detector. Scanning the voltages sweeps the transmitted mass across a range, producing a spectrum. Detectors used in such instruments include Faraday cups, which measure ion current directly, and electron multipliers, which amplify weak ion signals. The Apollo 17 LACE instead used a magnetic-deflection analyser. Gas molecules were ionised by electron bombardment, collimated, and passed through a magnetic field that separates them by mass before they reach the detector. The instrument's entrance aperture was oriented upward so that it measured the downward gas flux at the surface. The LADEE NMS is described in secondary summaries as having both open and closed ion sources. A closed source is reported to be better suited to species, such as helium and argon, that do not stick to ion-source surfaces. The primary instrument paper was not retrieved, so this description is recorded as secondary-reported.
article.scientific_importance: The lunar exosphere is too thin to behave like a conventional atmosphere, because its particles rarely collide with one another and instead follow ballistic paths over the surface. Its composition reflects a balance between sources, such as release from the interior, the solar wind and the surface regolith, and losses, such as thermal escape, photoionisation and acceleration by the solar wind electric field. Direct in-situ measurement of which species are present, and how their densities change between day and night and across latitude, is one of the few ways to test these processes. Records from LACE, NMS and CHACE-2 are therefore important for lunar science, even though each instrument sampled a different place, time and altitude and none provides a complete picture of the exosphere.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a neutral mass spectrometer. The three examples below use different analyser designs and were built for different missions. No mass, dimensions or power value for any of the three examples could be verified from a primary source during the preparation of this article, so those fields are recorded as null rather than estimated.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment (LACE)
examples.flight_status: Flown on Apollo 17 as part of the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), 1972-1973.
examples.mass_range_note: A secondary summary reports simultaneous detection of ions at 28 and 64 amu, with multiple mass ranges scanned by varying the electron-ion source voltage. A full mass range is not stated in the fetched NASA abstracts.
examples.operations: Deployed by the Apollo 17 astronauts at Taurus-Littrow, with the entrance aperture oriented upward. Turned on by ground command on 27 December 1972. Daytime operation was limited by high background gas levels. The sweep high voltage failed on 17 October 1973, during the tenth lunar month. Data were mainly collected at night.
examples.notes: Mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the fetched NASA abstracts. The full NASA-CR-150946 report was too large to parse, so no quantitative hardware values are recorded.

examples.name: LADEE Neutral Mass Spectrometer (NMS)
examples.flight_status: Flown on the Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer (LADEE), which orbited the Moon. Launch date and operational dates were not verified from primary sources; the 2011 abstract gave a planned early 2013 launch.
examples.instrument_class: Quadrupole mass spectrometer according to secondary summaries; the 2011 NASA abstract describes it only as a neutral mass spectrometer.
examples.mass_range_note: Secondary summaries report 1 to 150 u. This could not be checked against the primary instrument paper, which was not retrieved, so it is not used as a verified value.
examples.design_notes: Secondary summaries describe refurbished hardware from an earlier mission with a new ion optics design, and both open and closed ion sources, with the closed source suited to species such as helium and argon.
examples.reported_but_unverified: A secondary search summary reported a mass of about 11.3 kg and an average power of about 34.4 W. These could not be verified against the NASA Planetary Data System spacecraft document, which returned an access error, and they are not used in the structured fields.
examples.notes: The primary instrument paper (Mahaffy et al., 2014) and the results paper (Benna et al., 2015) were not retrieved. Their details are secondary-reported.

examples.name: Chandrayaan-2 CHACE-2
examples.type: Flown orbiter instrument on the Chandrayaan-2 mission
examples.flight_status: Onboard the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter. Observations were reported by ISRO and published in Geophysical Research Letters (2021).
examples.mass_range_note: Secondary search summaries of ISRO payload documentation report 1 to 300 amu. The ISRO page does not state a mass range, and the payload PDF could not be read, so this value is unverified.
examples.reported_but_unverified: Secondary summaries report a mass resolution of about 0.5 amu, an electron impact ionizer, a Bayard-Alpert gauge for total pressure, and Faraday cup and channel electron multiplier detectors. None of these could be checked against a primary source.
science_objectives: Map the global distribution of argon-40 in the lunar exosphere.
Study the dynamics of exospheric species.
Study radiogenic activity in the first few tens of metres below the surface.
examples.heritage: Successor to the CHACE experiment on the Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe; draws on the MENCA experiment on the Mars Orbiter Mission.
examples.notes: The ISRO page states the instrument type, objectives and results but not hardware specifications. The GRL article was not retrieved.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No verified external dimensions are available for any of the three examples, so none are recorded. The LACE was a miniature instrument; the LADEE NMS and CHACE-2 are described only by type and mission role in the sources consulted. The instruments' size and mounting depend on the analyser design, ionisation source, vacuum housing and the spacecraft or surface package in which they are installed. Any future instrument would need its dimensions set by its mass range, sensitivity, inlet geometry and mounting constraints.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No verified mass is recorded for any of the three examples. A secondary summary reported about 11.3 kg for the LADEE NMS, but this could not be verified against a primary source and is not used. Mass affects launch cost, orbiter or lander capacity, and structural support, so any new instrument would need a verified mass budget before integration.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No verified power value is recorded for any of the three examples. A secondary summary reported about 34.4 W average for the LADEE NMS, which could not be verified and is not used. The Apollo 17 LACE, which was part of a solar-powered ALSEP package, and CHACE-2, which operates as part of a spacecraft, would have power interfaces determined by their host systems. Power requirements for a new instrument must be set from its heater, electronics and pumping demands.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A neutral mass spectrometer on the lunar surface or in lunar orbit must operate in high vacuum, with extreme temperature variation, radiation exposure and micrometeoroid risk. Its own outgassing and the local gas environment both affect measurements. The Apollo 17 LACE was limited to night-time operation for much of its life because daytime sunrise produced high background gas levels, and it was paused during the day except for a brief check. Ion-source surfaces can also adsorb some species, which is why a closed source was reported for the LADEE NMS to measure species such as helium and argon more reliably. Measurement location and altitude matter greatly for an exospheric instrument. CHACE-2 measured argon-40 over equatorial and mid-latitude regions between minus 60 and plus 60 degrees latitude, and its observations showed diurnal variation, with densities rising near the sunrise terminator and reaching a minimum on the nightside.
article.limitations: A neutral mass spectrometer measures the species that reach its ion source at the altitude and time of observation. It does not measure the whole exosphere at once. Results depend on sensitivity, background gas levels, mass resolution and the instrument's position. Interpreting mass peaks can also be difficult when several species have similar masses, and an instrument that operates for a limited time can miss rare or episodic events. The LACE data were mainly collected at night, which limits the day-side picture. Quantitative hardware limits for the three examples have not been verified, so this article cannot give confident values for sensitivity or detection limits.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The three examples were delivered in different ways. LACE was a surface instrument delivered as part of the Apollo 17 ALSEP package. The LADEE NMS and CHACE-2 are orbiter instruments on lunar spacecraft.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into its host package or spacecraft on Earth.
Launch it on a launch vehicle and transfer it towards the Moon.
For surface instruments, deliver the package to the surface by lunar lander and deploy it by astronauts or mechanisms.
For orbiter instruments, perform orbit insertion, commissioning, and pointing, thermal and data-interface operations.
Connect power, thermal control and data systems to the host, then operate and calibrate the instrument.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LACE was deployed by the Apollo 17 astronauts at Taurus-Littrow on 12 December 1972, with its entrance aperture oriented upward during operation. The LADEE NMS and CHACE-2 were not deployed; they operated as spacecraft instruments. The LADEE NMS was part of a payload that also included an ultraviolet spectrometer and a dust detector, with a planned nominal periselene of 50 km according to the 2011 abstract.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 17 LACE is a historical surface example, delivered within the ALSEP package and operated for about ten lunations. The LADEE NMS and CHACE-2 are historical and current orbiter examples.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: This article does not assert compatibility with any named lander or spacecraft. Verified interface evidence, including mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, power and data interfaces, was not gathered for this payload, so compatibility cannot be assessed.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 17 LACE was among the first in-situ mass spectrometer measurements of the lunar atmosphere. It operated over ten lunations, and its data were mainly collected at night. The instrument reported that argon and helium were the dominant gases, that most lunar helium is of solar wind origin, and that methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide are present in very small amounts. Its sweep high voltage failed on 17 October 1973, during its tenth lunar month of operation. The LADEE NMS extended in-situ exosphere measurements into lunar orbit. Secondary summaries of its published results report that the exosphere is dominated by helium, argon and neon, and that argon abundance varied over time, possibly because of outgassing triggered by tidal stress. These summaries have not been checked against the primary papers. CHACE-2 produced the first reported global distribution of argon-40 in the exosphere, extending coverage to mid-latitudes between minus 60 and plus 60 degrees. ISRO links these observations to a 2021 Geophysical Research Letters publication. That article was not retrieved.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The LACE, NMS and CHACE-2 examples are not interchangeable, and their measurements were taken under different mission conditions. Mass, dimensions and power were not verified from primary sources for any of the three examples, so these fields are recorded as null rather than estimated. Some reported results come from secondary summaries whose primary papers could not be retrieved, and these are labelled as such in the article. The text is an engineering and scientific overview, not a certified design specification for a new neutral mass spectrometer.

data_quality_notes: Mass, dimensions and power are null for all three examples because no primary-source value was verified.

LADEE NMS mass (about 11.3 kg) and power (about 34.4 W) came from a single secondary search summary. The Spaceflight101 page it cited returned 404 and the NASA PDS spacecraft document returned 403, so the values were not used.

CHACE-2 mass range (1 to 300 amu) and resolution (about 0.5 amu) came from secondary search summaries of ISRO payload documentation. The ISRO CHACE-2 page does not state them and the payload PDF could not be read, so they are not recorded as verified.

LADEE NMS mass range (1 to 150 u), open and closed ion source description, and LADEE results (helium, argon and neon dominance; argon variability) come from secondary summaries. The primary papers (Mahaffy et al. 2014; Benna et al. 2015) were not retrieved.
The Apollo 17 LACE full report NASA-CR-150946 was too large to parse. Quantitative results are limited to the abstract.
Apollo 17 LACE recording accuracy (1%) and the 28 and 64 amu simultaneous detection come from Wikipedia, a secondary source.
The CHACE-2 Geophysical Research Letters article (2021) was not retrieved; authors and full results are not described beyond the ISRO page.
No image assets were verified, so this payload has no images and the registry is empty.
Lunar landing-site or location recommendations were not included, as deferred by the user.
